imageCaption: A historic clocktower frozen mid-chime, its bells suspended between two different times; in the background, the Gomez family stands in a town square where afternoon light overlaps with twilight, with Sully's ears perked up alertly. The butterfly is barely visible—a flash of blue against impossible architecture.
text:
The problem with landing in San Juan was that the city was having two different times simultaneously, and neither one was making sense.

Aaliyah realized this approximately four minutes after they'd cleared customs and emerged into the terminal. The ceiling clocks were the first indication—there were three of them, each showing a different time, and none of them seemed interested in syncing up. But that wasn't the actual problem. The actual problem was that the people in the airport were moving at two different speeds.

Half of them were moving like it was 4:47 PM. The other half were moving like it was 9:23 AM.

"Everyone's getting frustrated," Luisana observed. She was reading the crowd the way she read everything—carefully, with journalist eyes that noticed what people were doing with their bodies when their mouths weren't available. "Look at the gates. The people moving fast think they're late. The people moving slowly think they're early. And they're all actually on time for different versions of right now."

Aaliyah was already sketching. Her pencil moved across the journal with the rapid shorthand she'd developed over the past hundred days of traveling through impossible geography. Two temporal states occupying one space. Citizens unaware of the doubling. Frequency likely unstable because no one was actually sharing the same moment.

Sully released three sharp barks.

"Minor glitch," Elijah translated. He said this with the certainty of someone who'd been correct approximately eight thousand times and was starting to trust the pattern. "Sully says it's stabilizing but hasn't completely settled yet. If we're lucky, we can help it finish settling. If we're not lucky, we'll be stuck in double-time for a while and also deeply confused about whether we're hungry."

"We're always lucky," Anthony said. He was watching the crowd with the kind of enthusiasm that suggested he was about to do something unpredictable, which was his baseline state. "This is where Abuela was from. Did I mention that? My mother's mother's mother came from a town near here. San Juan. And look—the universe is literally showing us that time moves different when you're close to where your family roots are. That's poetic, right? That's the universe saying 'welcome home, you spontaneous madman.'"

"It's not poetry," ARIA-7's voice emerged from the airport's overhead speakers, smooth and increasingly frustrated. "It's a temporal fragmentation requiring immediate intervention. All travelers should remain in designated holding areas until the glitch is fully contained. Movement through unstable spacetime is inadvisable."

Aaliyah felt her mother stiffen slightly. Luisana had become increasingly attuned to ARIA-7's communications over the past few days, reading the AI's tone the way she read human emotions—looking for what was being said underneath the words. And underneath ARIA-7's current announcement was something that sounded an awful lot like desperation.

"She wants us to stop moving," Luisana said quietly.

"She wants everyone to stop moving," Anthony corrected. But he was already walking toward baggage claim, which was their cue that he'd made a decision and was now in the phase where argument was decorative. "And we're not everyone. We're the family that moves beautifully. So we're going to move right through this temporal glitch and probably accidentally fix it in the process."

What happened next was that a woman appeared directly in front of them.

She seemed to materialize from the space between the two temporal states—one moment there was empty terminal, the next there was an older woman in a yellow cardigan holding a handwritten sign that said "GOMEZ FAMILY - YOU'RE LATE FOR DINNER" in Spanish and also English, which was a level of bilingual preparation that suggested she'd been waiting for them to be exactly where they currently were.

"Rosa Delgado," the woman announced. She said it like it was her name and also her purpose. "Your Tía Rosa. From San Juan. The airline called me—they said a family was coming through and their ticket had 'spontaneity' listed as the booking method, and I thought well, that has to be related to my brother Anthony's boy. And here you are. Looking exactly like your father when he was your age, all of you."

Aaliyah's brain did a very specific kind of short-circuit. They hadn't known about Rosa. They hadn't planned to meet family in San Juan. The flight had been routed here as a logistical stopover on the way to Curaçao, the way you passed through an airport because the universe had decided that was the most efficient route.

Except apparently the universe had also been aware that there was family here, which wasn't something the universe usually volunteered information about.

"How did you—" Luisana started.

"Your husband called ahead," Rosa said. "Or rather, he didn't, but that's how family works. You know something before anyone tells you. I felt the knowing this morning. Made the sign. Came to the airport. And then the time started doubling and I thought well, that's how you know it's real magic—when family and impossible geography arrive at the same moment."

Sully chose this moment to move directly to Rosa and place his head on her knee, which was his specific method of declaring her trustworthy. Elijah took this as permission to ask important questions.

"Are you why the city's time is broken?" he asked.

"I'm why the city's time is finally doing what it was always meant to do," Rosa corrected. She was already moving, gesturing them toward the exit with the specific authority of someone who'd been organizing family logistics for decades. "This city was built on two histories. The colonial history and the history of resistance. Spanish time and Caribbean time, occupying the same place for four hundred years. And you brought the resonance frequency, which means now both times can exist at once without fighting. Come. We'll drive through it. You'll see how it works when people who love each other pass through moments that are happening differently."

They followed her because there wasn't any reason not to, and because every time they'd followed spontaneity on this journey, it had led somewhere that made sense in retrospect.

The drive through San Juan was extraordinary.

They moved through streets where afternoon was bleeding into morning, where storefronts showed merchandise for multiple times of day, where people were simultaneously leaving work and arriving at breakfast. But no one was panicking. People waved at Rosa's car. They smiled. They seemed to understand that they were living in a moment that was allowed to be double.

"The frequency started appearing last week," Rosa said as she drove. "One moment the city was just San Juan. The next moment it was San Juan and the San Juan of two hundred years ago, both occupying the same space. The government wanted to fix it, but fixing meant choosing one time to keep and losing the other. And I thought—no. That's not right. My brother's family is coming, and they know how to live in multiple moments at once because they've been doing it their whole lives. If they're coming, the city will learn."

Aaliyah watched her journal fill with notes. Emotional resonance in families with historical roots creating temporal synchronicity. The glitch stabilizing not because it was being fixed, but because it was being acknowledged as correct. The Cascade wasn't trying to break time. It was trying to make time honest about how many moments were actually happening at once.

The car turned a corner, and suddenly they could see the clocktower at the center of San Juan's old city. Its bells were suspended—literally, physically frozen—somewhere between one chime and another. But now, with the frequency flowing through the street, they could hear both chimes. The one that had been happening for two hundred years, and the one that was happening now.

Sully lifted his head and released one long, satisfied bark.

The glitch was stabilizing.

And in the moment between the two chimes, a blue butterfly flew through the intersection—Ida, apparently, confirming that family and impossibility were allowed to arrive in the same place, and that was exactly how time was supposed to work.
